title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 95–96
description: Curated advanced phrasal verbs, particle patterns, figurative connotations and cultural associations, with original examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided book. Vocabulary targets and usages are grounded in the teaching pages, exercises and answer key; all example sentences and notes are original. Textbook passages, exercise text and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 95 sections A–D and exercises 95.1–95.5; Unit 96 sections A–B, Language help and exercises 96.1–96.6; matching answer-key entries. Distinct phrasal-verb senses and culturally dependent associations are identified in notes.
audit.pronunciation: British English is the baseline. Broad IPA is provided only for selected short items where reasonably confident; longer expressions have empty IPA rather than speculative connected-speech transcriptions.
audit.languagePolicy: English only outside pt fields; all pt fields contain Brazilian Portuguese meanings.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared study pages, exercises, the Language help notes and relevant answer-key entries; independently wrote examples and explanatory notes, separated source targets from exercise-only targets and verified differences in meaning, register and verb patterns. Parsed the final JSON and checked schema parity, required fields, IDs, metadata and static speech-target constraints.
audit.limitations: No MP3 audio is included. Import into VocabLab, browser TTS pronunciation and speech recognition have not been tested. Connotations and superstitions are contextual cultural associations, not universal facts.

units.title: Unit 95 — Brushing up on phrasal verbs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 196–197 (PDF pages 198–199).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Vocabulary development · phrasal verbs and particle patterns
learningObjectives: Interpret phrasal verbs from context while keeping different senses distinct.
Distinguish related constructions with come and notice how a particle such as on contributes to meaning.
Use common workplace phrasal verbs with their correct particles and object placement.
Recognise additional exercise phrasal verbs and their register and usage constraints.

sectionsChecked: A · Learning phrasal verbs and meaningful alternatives
B · Phrasal verbs based on come
D · Workplace phrasal verbs and object-position guidance

items.example: The tutor recommended learning each phrasal verb in a meaningful context.
items.note: A verb combined with one or more particles or prepositions; meaning and grammar may be unpredictable.

items.example: I came across an old technical manual while clearing my desk.
items.note: In this sense come across means encounter something unexpectedly.

items.pt: passar a impressão de ser; parecer
items.example: Her short replies sometimes come across as dismissive.
items.note: Come across as + adjective or noun phrase describes an impression, not a chance discovery.

items.pt: parecer; transmitir a impressão de ser
items.example: During the interview, he came over as thoughtful and well prepared.
items.note: Close to come across as in the impression someone creates.

items.example: The research team put forward a proposal for a more reliable test procedure.
items.note: A separable phrasal verb: put forward a plan or put a plan forward.

items.example: Avoid rushing into a decision before the safety results are available.
items.note: Rush into + noun or -ing form suggests acting without sufficient thought.

items.example: The exhibition came off despite several last-minute problems.
items.note: Used for a plan or event that actually happens or succeeds.

items.pt: vir de outro lugar; deslocar-se até aqui
items.example: Several colleagues came over from Portugal to attend the workshop.
items.note: In this sense it describes movement towards the speaker’s location.

items.pt: dar em mim; o que me deu de repente
items.example: I do not know what came over me when I interrupted the speaker.
items.note: Often asks what caused an unusual, sudden change in behaviour.

items.pt: receber críticas; ser alvo de críticas
items.example: The policy came under criticism after the costs were published.
items.note: Come under + criticism, attack or pressure means be subjected to something unwelcome.

items.example: A rare opportunity to collaborate abroad came up last month.
items.note: Used for opportunities, issues or circumstances that arise.

items.example: We came up against serious compatibility issues during integration.
items.note: Usually followed by an obstacle, difficulty or opposition.

items.pt: permanecer; continuar em um local ou atividade
items.example: She stayed on at the institute to complete her research.
items.note: Stay on means remain beyond an expected departure or finishing point.

items.example: There is no benefit in dwelling on a mistake after you have corrected it.
items.note: Often used of repeatedly thinking about an unpleasant past event.

items.example: The new training format caught on faster than anyone expected.
items.note: Here it means become widely accepted or fashionable; not physically catching something.

items.pt: falar sem parar sobre; insistir em falar de
items.example: He kept going on about the delays during the entire journey.
items.note: Usually suggests that the listener is tired of repeated or lengthy talk.

items.example: The spectators urged the runners on during the final climb.
items.note: A separable construction: urge someone on, or urge on the runners.

items.example: Although the first prototype failed, the team pressed on.
items.note: Means continue resolutely despite obstacles.

items.example: Before the conference, she brushed up on her spoken English.
items.note: Improve knowledge or skills learnt earlier; brush up a skill is also possible.

items.example: The factory laid off temporary workers when orders fell.
items.note: A separable phrasal verb: lay off staff or lay staff off. Not the same as dismissing someone for misconduct.

items.example: Organisers called off the outdoor event because of severe weather.
items.note: Separable: call off a meeting or call a meeting off.

items.pt: dedicar-se de corpo e alma; empenhar-se intensamente em
items.example: She threw herself into developing the new testing framework.
items.note: The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject; followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.example: It took a few weeks for the new engineer to settle in.
items.note: Usually refers to becoming comfortable in a new workplace or home.

items.example: We put together a concise report from several independent measurements.
items.note: Separable: put together a report or put a report together.

items.pt: adaptar-se a um novo lugar ou rotina
items.example: The family quickly settled into life in their new city.
items.note: A related pattern with into followed by a noun phrase; do not use settle on for this meaning.

items.example: The committee proposed doing away with unnecessary paperwork.
items.note: Means abolish a rule, practice or object; not merely do without something.

items.pt: começar a fazer efeito; entrar em vigor
items.example: The updated safety rules will kick in at the beginning of November.
items.note: Informal; often used for rules, changes, systems or effects that begin operating.

items.pt: enrolar; perder tempo; ficar de brincadeira
items.example: Stop messing around and finish the checks before lunch.
items.note: Informal; in this context it means waste time rather than work seriously.

items.example: A few software bugs cropped up just before the demonstration.
items.note: Especially natural for unexpected problems or issues.

items.example: A shortage of components set the project back by three weeks.
items.note: Separable; set something back by a period expresses the length of delay.

items.example: The manager constantly ran down the work of junior staff.
items.note: Here it means speak critically or disparagingly; not run out of energy.

items.example: The technicians evacuated the area before the device could go off.
items.note: Used of a bomb or explosive device; the phrase has other senses in different contexts.

items.example: He held back an important detail during the investigation.
items.note: Separable: hold back information or hold information back.

units.title: Unit 96 — Connotation: making associations
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 198–199 (PDF pages 200–201).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Meaning and discourse · connotation, figurative associations and culture
learningObjectives: Differentiate literal meanings from figurative associations and connotations.
Recognise positive or negative connotations in political, advertising and interpersonal language.
Interpret conventional animal and colour associations without treating them as universal.
Understand luck-related cultural symbols and the limitations of cultural generalisations.

sectionsChecked: B · Understanding associations and Language help

items.pt: conotação; sentido associado a uma palavra
items.example: The word cheap can carry a negative connotation in advertising.
items.note: A feeling or idea suggested by a word in addition to its literal meaning.

items.example: Word associations can influence how an audience interprets a slogan.
items.note: Associations may be shared culturally or depend on an individual’s experience.

items.example: In the debate, the foreign minister was described as a dove.
items.note: A dove literally is a bird; in political language it can suggest a peacemaker, contrasting with hawk.

items.pt: pessoa linha-dura; defensor de posições agressivas
items.example: The commentator characterised the senator as a hawk on defence policy.
items.note: A figurative political hawk favours a forceful approach; the literal bird is a predator.

items.example: For many speakers, dogs symbolise faithfulness and companionship.
items.note: One conventional positive association of dogs; personal attitudes to animals differ.

items.pt: uma vida dura; vida muito infeliz
items.example: He described his years in the unsafe camp as a dog’s life.
items.note: An established expression for an unpleasant existence, despite positive associations of dogs.

items.pt: gato preto associado à sorte ou ao azar
items.example: Her grandmother considers seeing a black cat a sign of good luck.
items.note: The book contrasts traditionally positive associations in Britain with negative ones in the US; beliefs vary.

items.pt: visual parisiense; estilo elegante associado a Paris
items.example: The shop advertised a collection inspired by the Paris look.
items.note: An advertising association with glamour and fashion, not a technical clothing category.

items.example: They hired a cowboy builder who abandoned the renovation halfway through.
items.note: British informal, disapproving label for an unreliable or incompetent tradesperson.

items.pt: pessoa predatória ou inescrupulosa nos negócios
items.example: The sales adviser warned that the market had its share of sharks.
items.note: A figurative, negative use drawing on the animal’s dangerous reputation.

items.pt: uma cicatriz na paisagem; construção que desfigura o lugar
items.example: Residents called the abandoned concrete tower a scar on the landscape.
items.note: Strongly negative metaphor for a structure that spoils a place’s appearance.

items.pt: uma pessoa preciosa; alguém de grande valor humano
items.example: Our neighbour is a real diamond and helps whenever anyone is unwell.
items.note: Warm informal praise, using the value of a gemstone as a comparison.

items.example: The campaign relied on the glamour associated with old cinema.
items.note: Attractive sophistication or excitement; often exploited in advertising.

items.pt: roxo ou púrpura associado à realeza
items.example: The ceremony used purple fabric to suggest royal tradition.
items.note: Royalty is one conventional historical association of purple; it is not its only meaning.

items.example: The mentor realised that the newly appointed assistant was still rather green.
items.note: Figuratively inexperienced; green can also suggest nature, growth or environmental concern.

items.example: In the old novel, the villain calls his opponent yellow for refusing to fight.
items.note: A dated, insulting figurative use; colour associations are culturally and contextually variable.

items.example: The warning display used red to draw attention to a dangerous fault.
items.note: A common association with danger, though red has other possible associations.

items.example: The designer chose white to evoke simplicity and purity.
items.note: A conventional symbolic association in some contexts, not a universal rule.

items.pt: preto associado ao mal ou à escuridão
items.example: The story uses black as a conventional visual symbol of evil.
items.note: A traditional symbolic association, particularly in fiction; avoid treating it as inherent to the colour.

items.example: After the betrayal, he described his former partner as a snake.
items.note: A harsh, negative figurative label for someone considered deceitful.

items.example: The character is described as having mousy hair and a quiet manner.
items.note: Used especially of hair colour; its negative judgement about appearance is subjective.

items.example: She became ratty after waiting all afternoon for the delayed train.
items.note: Informal British English, describing an irritated or bad-tempered mood.

items.example: The interview contained several catty remarks about her colleagues.
items.note: Usually about remarks that are deliberately unkind or spiteful.

items.example: The accountant noticed something fishy about the missing receipts.
items.note: Informal: seeming dishonest or suspicious rather than literally smelling of fish.

items.pt: pessoa que segue os outros sem pensar por si
items.example: She refused to be a sheep and questioned the group’s decision.
items.note: Disapproving metaphor for an uncritical follower; the literal noun refers to the animal.

items.example: A hawk-eyed editor spotted a missing decimal point in the report.
items.note: Describes someone with exceptionally sharp eyesight or attention to detail.

items.example: She avoids travelling on Friday the thirteenth because she considers it unlucky.
items.note: A traditional bad-luck superstition, not a factual prediction.

items.example: They hung a horseshoe near the doorway as a traditional good-luck charm.
items.note: The horseshoe is commonly associated with good luck in the exercise.

items.pt: passar por baixo de uma escada (superstição de azar)
items.example: As a child, she was told not to walk under a ladder because it brought bad luck.
items.note: The superstition is the lexical/cultural point; in practice it can also be physically unsafe.

items.pt: trevo de quatro folhas; símbolo de boa sorte
items.example: He kept a pressed four-leaf clover in his notebook for good luck.
items.note: A conventional lucky symbol; the source also uses the variant four-leaved clover.
